duplicale
Feb. 4, 1937.
Dear Family:
Flying from Shanghai to Hongkong.
We had to wait at Shanghai for two hours account of heavy fog on the
river at our first port of call - Wenchow.
The first hundred miles
south of Shanghai is over flat country densely populated alluvial
delta land cross laced by innumerable small canals which serve alike
for transportation and for irrigation.
This country is all cultivated
is only rice,
a once a year crop in this section.
fields are bare and brown
new one not yet planted.
for the old crop has been harvested
We have just flown over Ningpo, important
treaty port open to foreign trade, famous for its sailors, missionaries
and Ningpo varnish which is used extensively by furniture
which when not properly dried will give tender skins a rash much like
poison ivy.
In Shanghai the pidgin English for "South" is "Ningpo more
far" which means any point below Ningpo.
As we fly "Ningpo more far"
the brown rice fields give way to low rolling country part rice and
part tea.
The tea bushes are planted in little terraced plots of
ground up
the mountainsides and from the air it is usually hard to
distinguish the rice land from
tea but at this time of year the tea
bushes remain green while the rice fielas are bare.
As we fly farther
South the mountains rise up to 4000 feet, jagged, sawtooth peaks cut
by mountain streams which erode great canyons through the tree-less
unprotected mountainsides, filling up with soil from the hillsides
narrow valleys which are
cultivated closely.
While forest volunteers
have attempted to recapture the mountains which once were theirs, the
Chinese peasants, for some reason unknown to me, light fires and
off all scrub timber even though no use is made
of the burnt over land.
Possibly they gather the charcoat or maybe they find protection against
bandits is improved by the elimination of cover - but whatever the
reason it seems almost criminal.
Messrs. Trippe and Whitney who have flown pretty much every-
where both said
that the scenic beauty of the flight from Hongkong to
Shanghai surpassed any they had seen elsewhere.
Great masses of stone,
narrow canyons cut from the solid rock, five hundred foot high
moss like hills and this
morning the valleys filled
in spots with fog the color of dirty cotton floating as though poured
the valleys by the Gods.
Here we are flying at 5000 feet in a
sunlit sky - no clouds, only
an Arizona blue in the dome from horizon
to horizon yet our last weather report from Wenchow reports
"ceiling
200 meters."
If the fog does not move out of our way - or there are
no holes through which we can fly down to land on the river, we shall
pass up Wenchow and continue on to Foochow.
We have just flown over Fenghua a small town where our aman
Ising Tzu came from and possibly more entitled to fame as the home of
Chiang Kai-shek, whose private airport lies below us.
The Generalissimo
is now there recuperating from his harrowing experiences at Sian-fu.
It is said on good authority that after his imprisonment at Sian-fu
he refused to confer with his captor Chang Hsueh-liang but quietly said
"You are my subordinate and will take orders from me, otherwise you are
a rebel and must shoot me - there is nothing else to be considered and
no reason for conferences."
Chiang Kai-shek is proud, fearless, ruth-
less yet patient.
He has given his life to the unification of China-
an almost,
if not entirely,
impossible task.
How heart sick, disillusion
ed and altogether miserable he must have been, caged, humiliated, and
bullied by a big headed, swashbuckling subordinate who was actuated by
motives almost wholly selfish.
It's the old old game of China.
player will sacrifice the right of individual action for the sake of
team play.
No player wants to run interference but each wants
the ball
every play and if anyone on his side is stupid enough
interference for him that's OK.
